title: Aluminium phosphide (celphos) poisoning
subject: toxicology
summary: Aluminium phosphide releases phosphine gas, causing refractory shock, toxic myocarditis and severe metabolic acidosis with very high mortality. There is no specific antidote: resuscitate aggressively with guided fluids and noradrenaline, correct acidosis, support organs, and consider rescue therapies (IABP, VA-ECMO); avoid water-based lavage and unproven remedies.

sections.title: Recognise
items: Grain fumigant tablets (usually 3 g, sold as celphos or 'rice tablets') release phosphine gas in contact with moisture and gastric acid; poisoning can also follow inhalation.
Early: vomiting, retrosternal and epigastric pain, restlessness, garlic or rotten fish odour. Within hours: shock with cold extremities, arrhythmias and severe metabolic acidosis.
Mortality is high (40 to 90% reported), mostly in the first 24 hours from refractory shock and arrhythmias; survivors usually recover cardiac function within days.
Other features: acute lung injury, methaemoglobinaemia, intravascular haemolysis (especially with G6PD deficiency), hypoglycaemia, oesophageal injury.
Confirmation if the history is unclear: silver nitrate paper test on gastric aspirate or breath turns black with phosphine; it also distinguishes herbal 'rice tablets'.

sections.title: Resuscitation
items: Remove from the exposure source and ventilate the room; staff should avoid inhaling fumes from vomitus or gastric aspirate. Wash contaminated skin and eyes with water.
High-flow oxygen; early intubation and ventilation for shock, acute lung injury or reduced consciousness.

Large-bore IV access, early central venous and arterial lines, continuous ECG. Give crystalloid boluses guided by CVP, echocardiography and lung ultrasound rather than large fixed volumes (capillary leak).
Persistent hypotension: noradrenaline (phenylephrine as an alternative or adjunct). Use dopamine and dobutamine cautiously because they provoke arrhythmias.
Keep antiarrhythmics, defibrillator and temporary pacing ready; correct potassium and magnesium.

sections.title: Investigations
items: Arterial blood gas with lactate, repeated every few hours; glucose (hourly initially), electrolytes including magnesium and potassium, renal and liver function, CBC.
ECG (arrhythmias, ST-T changes, conduction block) and echocardiography (global hypokinesia, low ejection fraction).
Co-oximetry for methaemoglobin if cyanosed despite oxygen; chest X-ray for pulmonary oedema or ARDS.

sections.title: Decontamination (limited role)
items: No gastric decontamination has proven benefit. ISCCM (2024) advises against gastric lavage and against carriers such as water, saline, oils and potassium permanganate.
Water-based fluids (water, milk, saline, permanganate) may liberate more phosphine; do not induce vomiting.
Some Indian centres give coconut oil or liquid paraffin orally to reduce phosphine release; support is limited to laboratory data and case reports.
Activated charcoal is unlikely to adsorb phosphine and is not routinely recommended.

sections.title: Supportive and adjunctive therapy
items: Metabolic acidosis: IV sodium bicarbonate for severe acidosis or as a bridge to dialysis; haemodialysis for refractory acidosis, AKI or fluid overload (it does not remove phosphine).
Symptomatic methaemoglobinaemia: methylene blue 1 to 2 mg/kg IV over 5 minutes, repeated if cyanosis persists; avoid with haemolysis or G6PD deficiency.

Magnesium sulfate is controversial: small studies reported lower mortality, but others found normal magnesium levels and no benefit. Correct documented hypomagnesaemia; high-dose routine use is unproven.
IV acetylcysteine (150 mg/kg over 1 hour, 50 mg/kg over 4 hours, 100 mg/kg over 16 hours) reduced mortality in a 2023 meta-analysis of 4 small RCTs; low-quality evidence, a reasonable adjunct.
High-dose insulin with glucose and IV lipid emulsion have been reported in small studies and case reports only.
Refractory cardiogenic shock: intra-aortic balloon pump or VA-ECMO where available, as myocardial injury is reversible in survivors.

sections.title: Monitoring and follow-up
items: ICU for all symptomatic patients: continuous ECG and arterial pressure, hourly urine output, serial lactate, blood gas and glucose.
Repeat echocardiography; in survivors function often normalises by about day 5.
Before discharge, if swallowing is difficult: barium swallow or upper GI endoscopy for oesophageal stricture or tracheo-oesophageal fistula. Psychiatric assessment for all intentional ingestions.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Potassium permanganate, water or repeated lavage that delays resuscitation and may release more phosphine.
Large unguided crystalloid volumes causing pulmonary oedema and serosal effusions.
Assuming death is inevitable and withholding full supportive care: the cardiac injury is reversible.
Missing co-ingested poisons or a herbal 'rice tablet' look-alike.

drugs.name: Noradrenaline (norepinephrine)
drugs.dose: Start 0.05 to 0.1 mcg/kg/min IV, titrate to MAP 65 mmHg

drugs.name: Sodium bicarbonate 8.4%
drugs.dose: IV boluses or infusion titrated to repeat blood gas
drugs.notes: Severe acidosis or bridge to dialysis; watch sodium and fluid load.

drugs.name: Methylene blue
drugs.dose: 1 to 2 mg/kg IV over 5 minutes, repeat if cyanosis persists
drugs.notes: Symptomatic methaemoglobinaemia; avoid in G6PD deficiency or haemolysis.

drugs.name: Acetylcysteine
drugs.dose: 150 mg/kg IV over 1 hour, then 50 mg/kg over 4 hours, then 100 mg/kg over 16 hours
drugs.notes: Adjunct; low-quality evidence of mortality benefit.

drugs.name: Magnesium sulfate
drugs.dose: Correct low magnesium; one reported regimen is 3 g IV over 3 hours, then 6 g per 24 hours for 3 to 5 days
